claims.text: In situ high-resolution TEM with an integrated heating stage can reveal atomic-scale structural changes in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles as temperature increases.
The detectable structural changes may include ordering transitions or phase segregation.
The as-synthesized AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The as-synthesized AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions.
Controlled in situ heating is applied during high-resolution TEM observation.
The nanoparticles are heated from ambient temperature to above 600 °C.
A high-vacuum or inert atmosphere minimizes extrinsic oxidation during heating.
Increasing temperature activates atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
Temperature-activated diffusion can produce ordering, segregation, or phase transitions at the nanoparticle scale.
Increasing thermal energy overcomes kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
The competition between configurational entropy and enthalpic contributions governs the evolution of the nanoparticles' atomic structure at elevated temperature.
In situ heating will produce observable discrete atomic rearrangements, including ordered-domain formation or the onset of compositional segregation.
Thermodynamic contributions have been theoretically predicted to enhance the thermal stability of high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced thermal stability has not been directly verified at atomic scale in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Nanoparticle size, electron-beam exposure, heating rate, and atmosphere may influence the observed effects.
High-resolution TEM images can monitor atomic ordering and morphology.
Electron diffraction patterns can identify phase transitions or segregation.
